Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

Include **manual security audits** such as penetration testing and may address broader regulatory requirements (GDPR, KRITIS, NIS2, SGB). - Results are also entered into the technical‑debt Jira project, but the audit itself provides an **objective, third‑party validation** of security and compliance. **How they differ** | Aspect | Internal Audit | External Audit | |--------|----------------|----------------| | **Who performs it** | Internal staff (Head of Engineering, lead/senior developers) | Independent external security advisors/partners | | **When/How often** | Continuous, tied to development milestones and regular internal meetings | Periodic (often annually or semi‑annually) and on‑demand | | **Tools & Methods** | AWS Well‑Architected self‑service checks, PR reviews, internal design reviews | External tooling/services, manual penetration testing, third‑party compliance checks | | **Scope** | Design verification, architectural guardrails, day‑to‑day compliance | Full‑system security assessment, regulatory compliance, unbiased validation | | **Purpose** | Ensure internal standards are met and guide immediate remediation | Provide an independent view, uncover hidden risks, and satisfy external compliance requirements | In short, **internal audits** are the organization’s own, ongoing checks embedded in the development workflow, while **external audits** are independent, periodic examinations performed by third parties to validate security and compliance from an outside perspective. Both feed findings into the same technical‑debt tracking system, but they differ in origin, frequency, methodology, and overall purpose.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

1. **Relevant Information from the Context**:  
   - The use of third-party software and services must avoid legal issues, ensure proven value, and prevent lock-in or end-of-life (EoL) risks.  
   - Due to handling GDPR-regulated data, the **geographic location** of services and their **data privacy agreements** are critical.  
   - Services run by third-party providers may need to be listed in **Data Processing Agreements (DPAs)** between virtualQ and its clients.  
   - **Licenses and IP ownership** are evaluated, especially for open-source components.  
   - Not all open-source licenses are compatible with virtualQ’s requirements, particularly regarding privacy and data access.  
   - For certain customers (e.g., those under **SGB** or **KRITIS**), requirements exceed standard certifications like **C5**, **PCI-DSS**, **HIPAA**, or **ISO 27xxx**.  
   - Example: AWS RDS, while C5-compliant, cannot be used directly for SGB-regulated data because AWS, as a managed service provider, could theoretically access plain-text data.  
   - Therefore, **sensitive data must be encrypted** using customer-managed keys to ensure no third party (including cloud providers) can access it in plaintext.  
   - Key legal and compliance questions include:  
     - Is data encrypted at rest and in transit?  
     - Who can access the data, and is there a legitimate business reason?  
     - Can the effectiveness of security measures be proven?  
     - Are there additional requirements from GDPR, SGB, or KRITIS?

2. **How These Connect**:

This includes ensuring that no third party (even cloud providers) can access unencrypted data, and that all data processing can be legally justified and documented in DPAs.

3. **Conclusion**:  
   The legal criteria for third-party software and services are not just about the license type or general compliance certifications, but about **ensuring full control over data access, meeting strict regulatory requirements (beyond standard certifications), and being able to legally justify and document all data processing activities**.

---

**Final Answer**:  
The legal criteria for third-party software and services include:  
- Ensuring **data is encrypted at rest and in transit**, preferably with keys managed by virtualQ to prevent unauthorized access.  
- Verifying the **geographic location** of data storage and processing to comply with EU GDPR and national regulations (e.g., SGB).  
- Confirming that **no third party (including service providers) can access plain-text data**, even in theory.  
- Evaluating **licenses and intellectual property (IP) ownership**, especially for open-source components, to avoid legal conflicts.  
- Ensuring the service can be included in **Data Processing Agreements (DPAs)** with clients, particularly for GDPR, SGB, and KRITIS-regulated customers.  
- Validating compliance with relevant standards (e.g., C5, ISO 27001), while recognizing that **some customers require stricter controls beyond certification**.  
- Being able to **prove the effectiveness of security and privacy measures** through audits or technical evidence.

1. **Relevant Information from the Context:**

- **Internal Audits & Design Verification:**
  - Occur during implementation when decisions must be made between different implementation options.
  - Smaller decisions are handled by engineers and verified via pull request reviews.
  - Larger, strategic, or architectural decisions are made in dedicated internal meetings.
  - The **AWS Well-Architected Framework** is used as a self-service audit tool for cloud or hybrid infrastructure.
  - This audit evaluates six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, and Sustainability.
  - It identifies where implementations diverge from best practices.
  - Conducted once or twice a year.
  - Findings are tracked as **technical debt** and followed up based on criticality.
  - Participants: Head of Engineering, Lead Developer, senior developers as needed.

- **External Audits:**
  - Based on external tooling/services that verify the virtualQ system, either in the codebase or in a non-production live system.
  - Include manual security audits such as **penetration testing**, carried out by a partner.
  - External reviews are carried out **regularly**.
  - Findings are reported and added to the **technical debt Jira project** for follow-up.
  - Also mentioned: further details can be found in “IT Infrastructure, Security & Compliance”.

2. **How These Pieces Connect:**

- Both internal and external audits aim to ensure system **security, compliance, and quality**.
- Both result in findings that are **tracked as technical debt** and followed up accordingly.
- Both types of audits support **continuous improvement** and **risk mitigation**.
- However, they differ in **origin, scope, methodology, and participants**:
  - **Internal audits** are organization-led, often using frameworks like AWS Well-Architected, focusing on architectural best practices and design decisions.
  - **External audits** are conducted by third parties using tools or manual testing (e.g., penetration tests), focusing on objective, outside-in validation of security and system integrity.

3. **Conclusion:**

Internal audits are **proactive, strategy-focused evaluations** conducted by internal teams using structured frameworks (like AWS Well-Architected) to assess architecture and design decisions. They occur periodically and emphasize alignment with best practices across multiple operational pillars.

External audits are **independent assessments** performed by third-party tools or partners, focusing on code and system security through automated scans and penetration testing. They provide an objective, external perspective on vulnerabilities and compliance.

The key difference lies in **who conducts them** (internal team vs. external parties), **their focus** (design/architecture vs. security/testing), and **methodology** (self-assessment vs. external verification).

---

**Final Answer:**

**Internal audits** are evaluations led by the organization’s own team—such as the Head of Engineering and senior developers—using frameworks like the AWS Well-Architected Tool to assess system design and architecture across pillars like security, reliability, and cost efficiency. They occur once or twice a year and focus on strategic decision-making and adherence to best practices, with findings tracked as technical debt.

**External audits** involve third-party tools or partners conducting security verification on the virtualQ system, either in the codebase or non-production environments, including manual penetration testing. These are performed regularly and provide an independent assessment of system security and compliance.

**The main differences** are:
- **Conducted by**: Internal team vs. external parties.
- **Focus**: Architectural design and operational best practices (internal) vs. security testing and vulnerability detection (external).
- **Method**: Self-assessment using structured frameworks vs. independent testing and tool-based scanning.
- **Frequency**: Periodic (1–2 times/year) vs. regular/recurring as needed.

Both feed into technical debt tracking for follow-up actions.

In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots. 
Zusammenfassung: 
Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

**Legal Criteria for Using 3rd‑Party Software (or Services)** When evaluating any external library, tool, or cloud service, the following legal‑compliance questions must be answered before the component can be approved for the virtualQ platform: | Area | Specific criterion | Why it matters | |------|--------------------|----------------| | **Data‑Protection & Privacy** | • The provider must comply with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
• The service’s **geographic location** (data‑center / processing region) must meet the required data‑residency rules for the customer’s jurisdiction.
• A **Data‑Processing Agreement (DPA)** must be in place (and the provider must be listed in the DPA that virtualQ shares with its clients). | Guarantees that personal / regulated data is handled lawfully and that virtualQ can demonstrate compliance to its customers. | | **Sector‑Specific Regulatory Fit** | • The service must be eligible for the specific security‑certification program required by the customer (e.g. **C5** for German federal‑government cloud, **PCI‑DSS**, **HIPAA**, **ISO/IEC 27000‑series**, **SGB** for social‑law data, **KRITIS** for critical‑infrastructure).
• If the provider is a *managed* service (e.g., AWS RDS), confirm that the provider cannot read plain‑text data (encryption, key‑ownership, zero‑knowledge guarantees). | Some customers (public‑sector, health, finance, critical‑infrastructure) can only use services that are explicitly certified for their regime. | | **Encryption & Access Controls** | • Data must be **encrypted at rest** and **encrypted in transit** using industry‑standard algorithms.
• Encryption keys must be under virtualQ’s (or the customer’s) control; the 3rd‑party must not have unrestricted access to clear‑text data.
• A clear business justification must exist for any party (including the provider’s staff) that can view the data. | Prevents unauthorized reading of regulated data and satisfies GDPR Art. 32 (security of processing). | | **Proof of Security Effectiveness** | • The provider must be able to supply **independent audit reports** (SOC 2, ISO 27001, C5 audit, penetration‑test results, etc.).
• virtualQ must be able to **demonstrate** that the provider’s security controls are effective (e.g., test reports, certifications, continuous monitoring). | Enables virtualQ to prove to regulators and customers that the security posture is adequate. | | **Licensing & IP Ownership** | • All open‑source components must be under licences that are **compatible with virtualQ’s distribution model** (e.g., Apache 2.0, MIT are generally safe; GPL‑v3 may impose copyleft obligations).
• The licence terms must not impose **additional obligations** (e.g., source‑code disclosure, patent retaliation) that conflict with virtualQ’s business model.
• For proprietary software, verify that the **license grant** covers the intended usage (internal, commercial, redistribution) and that there are no hidden **royalty** or **restriction** clauses. | Prevents legal disputes over IP, ensures that virtualQ can legally ship and maintain the software, and avoids accidental introduction of copyleft obligations. | | **Vendor Lock‑in & End‑of‑Life (EoL)** | • The contract should include **exit clauses**, data‑migration guarantees, and **source‑code or artifact** hand‑over provisions if the service is discontinued.
• Check the provider’s **road‑map** and **support lifecycle** to avoid being stranded when the product reaches EoL. | Reduces operational risk and protects the ability to switch providers without breaching contracts. | | **Compliance Documentation** | • The provider must furnish **up‑to‑date compliance documentation** (privacy policy, security white‑papers, audit certificates).
• All documentation must be **reviewable** by virtualQ’s legal/compliance teams and retained for audit purposes. | Enables internal and external auditors to verify that the third‑party component meets all required legal standards. | ### How to Apply the Criteria (Step‑by‑Step) 1. **Identify the data type** that will flow through the third‑party component (personal data, health data, critical‑infrastructure data, etc.). 2. **Map the regulatory regime** that applies to that data (GDPR + any sector‑specific rules such as SGB, KRITIS, C5, PCI‑DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27xxx). 3. **Check the provider’s certifications** and DPA inclusion against the required regime. 4. **Review the licensing** of any software libraries: * Is the licence compatible with virtualQ’s commercial use? * Are there any copyleft or patent clauses that could affect IP ownership? 5. **Validate encryption & key‑management** – confirm that data is encrypted at rest/in‑transit and that virtualQ (or the customer) retains control of the encryption keys. 6. **Obtain and assess audit evidence** (SOC 2, ISO 27001, C5 audit reports, penetration‑test results) to prove security effectiveness. 7. **Confirm contractual safeguards** for data access, exit, and continuity (no hidden data‑access rights for the vendor, clear termination and data‑migration terms). 8. **Document the findings** in a compliance checklist that can be reviewed by internal/legal teams and used in future audits. --- **Bottom line:** The legal criteria for any 3rd‑party software/service are a combination of **data‑protection compliance (GDPR & sector‑specific rules), licensing/IP compatibility, encryption & access controls, demonstrable security certifications, and contractual provisions that prevent lock‑in and ensure a clean exit**. Only when all these points are satisfied can the component be safely integrated into the virtualQ system.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
**Answer**

### 1. What the context tells us  

| Aspect | Internal Audits & Design Verification | External Audits |
|--------|----------------------------------------|-----------------|
| **Who carries them out?** | Head of Engineering, Lead Developer, senior developers (and sometimes the whole engineering team). | External security advisor, specialised partners, third‑party tooling/services. |
| **When are they performed?** | Regular decision‑point meetings during implementation; a self‑service “AWS Well‑Architected” audit once or twice a year; continuous peer‑review of pull‑requests. | Scheduled external reviews (e.g., penetration‑testing, compliance checks) on a regular basis; ad‑hoc scans of the code base or live (non‑production) system. |
| **What do they look at?** | Architectural guardrails, strategic design choices, compliance with internal best‑practice pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability). | Compliance with external regulations (GDPR, KRITIS, NIS2, SGB), security posture of the whole stack, vulnerability findings from independent tools/services. |
| **How are findings handled?** | Findings become “technical debt” items in an internal Jira project; they are prioritised and resolved according to criticality. | Findings are also entered into the same technical‑debt Jira project so they are tracked and followed up, but the remediation plan is usually driven by the external partner’s recommendations. |
| **Purpose** | Ensure the product is built according to the organisation’s own architectural and quality standards; provide early detection of design flaws; keep internal technical debt under control. | Provide an independent, objective assessment of security and regulatory compliance; validate that the system would stand up to an outside attacker or regulator. |

### 2. How the pieces connect  

- Both audit types feed into a **single technical‑debt tracking system** (Jira), which guarantees that any issue—whether raised internally or externally—is visible, prioritised, and eventually fixed.  
- **Internal audits** are mainly **process‑oriented** (code reviews, design meetings, AWS Well‑Architected checks) and are driven by people who build the system.  
- **External audits** are **product‑oriented** and **independent**: they use third‑party tools or consultants to evaluate the system from the outside, often with a stronger emphasis on regulatory compliance and penetration‑testing.

### 3. Conclusion – Definition and Differences  

**Internal Audits**  
- Conducted by the organization’s own staff (engineering leadership and developers).  
- Embedded in the development lifecycle (pull‑request reviews, architecture decision meetings, periodic AWS Well‑Architected reviews).  
- Focus on internal design guardrails, best‑practice adherence, and early detection of technical debt.  
- Frequency is typically “continuous” with a formal audit once or twice a year.

**External Audits**  
- Performed by independent third parties (security advisors, audit firms, specialised tooling providers).  
- Usually scheduled at regular intervals or triggered by compliance calendars.  
- Emphasise objective verification of security, privacy, and regulatory compliance (GDPR, KRITIS, NIS2, SGB) through penetration testing, code‑base scans, and live‑system assessments.  
- Findings are external validations that must be addressed, often with a higher level of scrutiny because they come from outside the organization.

**Key Differences**  

| Dimension | Internal Audits | External Audits |
|-----------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Who** | Internal engineers & leaders | Independent external experts/companies |
| **Perspective** | “Inside‑looking” – aligns with internal standards & roadmap | “Outside‑looking” – validates against external standards & attacker view |
| **Scope** | Design decisions, code quality, internal best‑practice pillars | Security posture, regulatory compliance, vulnerability exposure |
| **Control** | Organization controls timing, depth, and remediation | Organization must respond to third‑party reports; often more formal remediation timelines |
| **Objective** | Continuous improvement, technical‑debt management | Independent assurance, compliance certification, risk reduction |

In short, **internal audits** are an ongoing, self‑governed quality‑control process, while **external audits** are periodic, independent assessments that provide an unbiased view of security and compliance. Both are essential: internal audits keep the team aligned and the code clean; external audits give confidence to regulators, customers, and stakeholders that the system meets the required legal and security standards.

They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

- Third-party services may need to be included in **Data Processing Agreements (DPAs)** with virtualQ’s clients.
- **Licenses and IP ownership** are evaluated, especially for open-source components, due to varying legal obligations depending on license type.
- Compliance can be inherited by using services within scope of recognized standards (e.g., C5, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27xxx), but this may not suffice for SGB or KRITIS.

2. **How These Pieces Connect:**

The legal criteria are driven by the type of data handled (GDPR, SGB, KRITIS-sensitive) and the potential for third parties—whether cloud providers or open-source maintainers—to access or affect that data. Legal compliance is not just about using compliant services but ensuring that contractual, technical, and jurisdictional safeguards prevent unauthorized access. This includes assessing where data resides, who can access it (even in theory), and whether required certifications or DPAs are in place.

3. **Conclusion:**

The legal criteria for third-party software and services are centered on data protection, regulatory compliance, contractual obligations, and intellectual property. These criteria ensure that virtualQ remains compliant with strict legal standards, particularly for sensitive sectors.

---

**Final Answer:**

The legal criteria for third-party software and services include:

- **Data Privacy & Jurisdiction:** Ensuring the geographic location of services and their data processing practices comply with GDPR and other applicable regulations (e.g., SGB, KRITIS).
- **Data Access Control:** Confirming that no third party (including service providers) can access data—even in theory—without justification and safeguards (e.g., encryption prevents provider access).
- **Data Processing Agreements (DPAs):** Third-party services that process personal data must be suitable for inclusion in DPAs with virtualQ’s clients.
- **Compliance Certifications:** Preference for services compliant with recognized standards (e.g., C5, ISO 27001, HIPAA), though additional safeguards may be needed for high-assurance sectors like SGB or KRITIS.
- **Licensing & IP Ownership:** Open-source components must be evaluated for license compatibility to avoid legal risks (e.g., copyleft licenses that could affect proprietary code).
- **Encryption Requirements:** Data must be encrypted both at rest and in transit, with keys managed to prevent third-party access.

These criteria ensure legal compliance, protect sensitive data, and mitigate regulatory and contractual risks when integrating third-party software or services.

**1. Relevant Information from the Context:**

- **Internal Audits & Design Verification:**
  - Occur during implementation when decisions must be made about how to build features.
  - Smaller decisions are handled by engineers and verified via pull request reviews.
  - Larger, strategic, or architectural decisions are made in dedicated internal meetings.
  - Includes use of the **AWS Well-Architected Framework**, a self-service audit tool assessing six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, and Sustainability.
  - These audits are conducted **once or twice a year**.
  - Findings are tracked as **technical debt** and followed up based on criticality.
  - Participants: Head of Engineering, Lead Developer, and senior developers as needed.

- **External Audits:**
  - Conducted by **external partners or services**.
  - Involve **tool-based verification** of the virtualQ system (code base or non-production live systems).
  - Include **manual security audits**, such as **penetration testing**, performed by a partner.
  - Also carried out **on a regular basis**.
  - Findings are reported and added to the **technical debt Jira project** for tracking and follow-up.
  - Linked to compliance requirements like GDPR, KRITIS, NIS2, SGB.

- **Additional Context:**
  - Both internal and external audits contribute to identifying technical debt.
  - Regular meetings (involving CEO, Head of Engineering, external security advisor) help define strategic roadmaps, especially around compliance.

**2. How These Pieces Connect:**

- Both internal and external audits aim to **ensure system security, compliance, and architectural soundness**.
- Both result in findings that are **tracked as technical debt** and prioritized for resolution.
- They differ primarily in **who conducts them** and **their focus/methods**:
  - **Internal audits** are **self-assessments** led by the engineering team using frameworks like AWS Well-Architected, focusing on architecture and design decisions.
  - **External audits** are **independent evaluations** by third parties using tools and manual testing (e.g., penetration tests), focusing on security and compliance in code and live systems.

**3. Conclusion:**

Internal and external audits are complementary processes: internal audits focus on **design integrity and architectural best practices** during development, while external audits provide **independent validation of security and compliance** post-development or in staging environments.

---

**Final Answer:**

**Internal audits** are self-conducted assessments (e.g., using the AWS Well-Architected Framework) by the company’s engineering leadership to evaluate architectural decisions, design quality, and adherence to best practices. They occur 1–2 times per year and focus on strategic system design across pillars like security, reliability, and cost efficiency. Findings are managed as technical debt.

**External audits** are independent evaluations performed by third-party partners or tools to verify the security and compliance of the virtualQ system—both in code and in non-production environments. These include automated scans and manual penetration testing, and are conducted regularly.

**Key Differences:**
- **Conducted by:** Internal audits are done by internal staff; external audits by third parties.
- **Focus:** Internal audits emphasize architectural and design decisions; external audits emphasize security vulnerabilities and compliance.
- **Method:** Internal audits use self-assessment frameworks; external audits use tooling and manual penetration testing.
- **Trigger & Frequency:** Internal audits are periodic (annual/biannual); external audits are ongoing or regularly scheduled.

Both types of findings are tracked in the technical debt system for follow-up.

Demo | Beschreibung | Einrichtung | Ansagen | BETA BETRIEB | Pricing | Verwandte Themen
Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots. 
Zusammenfassung: 
Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots. 
Zusammenfassung: 
Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

**Legal criteria for using a 3rd‑party software or service (as defined in the virtualQ document)** | # | Criterion | What it means in practice | Why it matters | |---|-----------|---------------------------|----------------| | 1 | **GDPR compliance** | – The provider must respect the EU General Data Protection Regulation – data‑subject rights, lawful basis for processing, records of processing activities, breach‑notification obligations, etc.
– The provider’s privacy policy and contractual clauses (e.g., Standard Contractual Clauses or EU‑US Data‑Transfer Agreements) must be available and acceptable. | VirtualQ processes personal data of EU citizens; non‑compliance would expose both parties to fines and reputational damage. | | 2 | **Sector‑specific regulatory fit** | – For customers subject to **SGB (German Social Code)**, **KRITIS (critical infrastructure)**, **C5 (BSI Cloud‑Computing‑Compliance‑Catalogue)**, **PCI‑DSS**, **HIPAA**, **ISO/IEC 27xxx** etc., the service must be explicitly listed as “in‑scope” for the relevant certification or be able to meet the same controls through compensating measures (e.g., client‑side encryption). | These regimes impose stricter technical‑organizational requirements (e.g., encryption, auditability) that go beyond baseline GDPR. | | 3 | **Data‑location / geo‑restriction** | – The physical location of the data‑centers (or the ability to restrict them) must be known and must satisfy any residency requirements of the customer or regulator (e.g., EU‑only storage for GDPR‑sensitive data). | Cross‑border transfers trigger additional legal mechanisms; many public‑sector contracts forbid data leaving the EU. | | 4 | **Data‑access & confidentiality guarantees** | – Clear contractual statements on who (employees, subcontractors, government agencies) can access the raw data and under which business‑justified circumstances.
– Ability to enforce “need‑to‑know” and “zero‑knowledge” (e.g., encryption where the provider cannot see plaintext). | Prevents inadvertent or illegal inspection of confidential or regulated data (e.g., AWS RDS is not acceptable for SGB customers because AWS could view plaintext). | | 5 | **Encryption at rest & in transit** | – The provider must support strong encryption (e.g., AES‑256) for stored data and TLS 1.2/1.3 for data in motion, or the customer must apply an additional encryption layer that the provider cannot decrypt. | Encryption is a core GDPR safeguard and often a mandatory technical control for SGB/KRITIS. | | 6 | **Proof of security effectiveness** | – Availability of audit reports, penetration‑test results, third‑party certifications (C5, ISO 27001/27017/27018, SOC 2, etc.).
– Ability to obtain evidence that controls are operating as claimed (e.g., logs, attestation letters). | Enables virtualQ to demonstrate due‑diligence to its own clients and regulators. | | 7 | **License compatibility & IP ownership** | – The software’s open‑source or proprietary license must allow the intended use, redistribution, modification, and integration into virtualQ’s product.
– No “viral” (e.g., GPL‑v3) or restrictive clauses that would force virtualQ to disclose its own source code or impose additional obligations.
– Clear statement of who owns any contributed IP and that virtualQ retains a royalty‑free, worldwide licence. | Violating license terms can lead to legal claims, loss of IP, or forced open‑sourcing of proprietary code. | | 8 | **Inclusion in the Data‑Processing Agreement (DPA)** | – The third‑party must be listed as a sub‑processor in virtualQ’s DPA with clients, and the DPA must contain the required clauses (processor obligations, audit rights, breach notification, etc.). | Clients demand visibility of every entity that may process their data; omission can breach contractual obligations. | | 9 | **Vendor lock‑in / End‑of‑Life (EoL) considerations** | – Ability to export data in a standard, portable format.
– Clear termination clauses, notice periods, and support for migration to an alternative solution. | Prevents a “dead‑end” where virtualQ cannot replace the service without massive re‑engineering or data loss. | |10| **Operational risk & liability** | – Contractual allocation of liability for data breaches, non‑compliance fines, and indemnification.
– Insurance (e.g., cyber‑risk policies) covering the provider’s operations. | Ensures that financial risk is manageable and that the provider can cover damages arising from its failures. | --- ### How the criteria were derived (step‑by‑step) 1. **Identify the regulatory backdrop** – The text repeatedly stresses GDPR, SGB, KRITIS, and BSI‑C5 as the primary legal frameworks governing the data that virtualQ handles. 2. **Extract the concrete legal questions** – The “Important questions to ask” list (encryption, who can view data, proof of security, additional technical/organizational requirements) directly translates into legal compliance checkpoints. 3. **Add the licensing/IP dimension** – The document mentions that “licenses and IP ownership are evaluated” and that “not every open source …” is suitable, indicating that licence compatibility is a legal criterion. 4. **Consider contractual and operational aspects** – The need to list 3rd‑party providers in DPAs, avoid lock‑in, and manage liability are explicitly discussed elsewhere in the broader risk‑assessment sections. 5. **Combine all points** – Group the extracted items into a coherent checklist that covers data‑protection law, sector‑specific rules, data residency, access controls, encryption, auditability, licensing, DPA inclusion, vendor lock‑in, and liability. --- ### Bottom line When evaluating any 3rd‑party software or service, virtualQ must verify that it satisfies **(1) GDPR and any sector‑specific regulatory requirements (SGB, KRITIS, C5, PCI‑DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27xxx, etc.)**, **(2) data‑location and encryption safeguards**, **(3) clear, limited data‑access provisions**, **(4) provable security controls**, **(5) compatible licensing and clear IP ownership**, **(6) inclusion as a sub‑processor in the DPA**, **(7) manageable exit/lock‑in conditions**, and **(8) appropriate contractual liability and insurance**. Only when all of these legal criteria are met can the third‑party component be safely integrated into the virtualQ ecosystem.

**Answer** ### 1. What the context tells us | Aspect | Internal Audits (as described) | External Audits (as described) | |--------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------| | **Who performs them** | Head of Engineering, Lead Developer, senior developers, other internal staff; sometimes aided by internal tools (e.g., AWS Well‑Architected Framework). | External security advisor, third‑party partners, specialised tooling/services that are not owned by the company. | | **When they happen** | During implementation at “decision points”; regularly (once or twice a year) via the AWS Well‑Architected self‑service audit; also as part of regular internal design‑verification meetings. | On a regular, scheduled basis (e.g., quarterly, annually) and ad‑hoc after major releases; penetration‑testing engagements are carried out by a partner. | | **What they examine** | Architecture guardrails, strategic design choices, compliance with internal best‑practice guidelines, coverage of existing modules, UI‑framework testability, technical‑debt items. | The actual code base and live (non‑production) system using external tools/services; security posture, vulnerability findings, compliance with regulations (GDPR, KRITIS, NIS2, SGB). | | **How findings are handled** | Findings are recorded as technical‑debt items in an internal Jira project, prioritized by criticality, and addressed by the development teams. | Findings are also entered into the same technical‑debt Jira project so they can be tracked, but the remediation plan is often driven by the external partner’s recommendations and may involve contractual obligations. | | **Typical artifacts** | AWS Well‑Architected Framework report (covers Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability).
Internal design‑verification minutes, pull‑request reviews. | External audit reports, penetration‑test results, compliance certifications, third‑party tool scan outputs. | ### 2. How the pieces connect - **Purpose overlap** – Both audit types aim to ensure that the *virtualQ* system is secure, reliable, and compliant. - **Different lenses** – Internal audits look at *how the team builds and governs* the system (processes, architectural decisions, internal standards). External audits look at *what the system actually looks like from the outside* (code quality, runtime security, regulatory compliance) using independent expertise. - **Feedback loop** – Results from external audits are fed back into the internal audit/technical‑debt process, influencing future internal design‑verification meetings and the AWS Well‑Architected review. ### 3. Conclusion – Definition and key differences **Internal Audits** - Conducted by the organization’s own staff (engineering leadership, senior developers, etc.). - Focus on internal processes, design decisions, adherence to the company’s architectural guardrails, and self‑assessment frameworks (e.g., AWS Well‑Architected). - Findings become internal technical‑debt items that the same teams are responsible for fixing. **External Audits** - Performed by independent third parties (external security advisors, penetration‑testing partners, specialised tooling providers). - Examine the actual product (code, live non‑production environment) against external standards, regulations, and industry best practices. - Results are also recorded as technical‑debt, but remediation may be driven by contractual obligations, external recommendations, or compliance deadlines. **Key Differences** | Dimension | Internal Audit | External Audit | |-----------|----------------|----------------| | **Performed by** | Internal staff | Independent third‑party experts | | **Primary focus** | Process, architecture, internal standards | Product security, regulatory compliance, external best‑practice validation | | **Tooling** | AWS Well‑Architected self‑service, internal checklists, pull‑request reviews | External scanning tools, penetration‑testing suites, compliance audit frameworks | | **Frequency & trigger** | Regular decision‑point meetings, annual AWS review | Regular scheduled external reviews, ad‑hoc after releases | | **Outcome ownership** | Development teams own remediation | May involve external partners; remediation still tracked internally but guided by external advice | In short, **internal audits** are *self‑governance* activities that ensure the team follows its own rules and architectural guidelines, while **external audits** are *independent validations* that test the system against outside standards and regulations. Both feed into the same technical‑debt tracking system but differ in who conducts them, what they examine, and how the results are acted upon.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

1. **Relevant Information from the Context**:  
   - The use of third-party software and services must avoid legal issues, ensure proven value, and prevent lock-in or end-of-life (EoL) risks.  
   - Due to GDPR, SGB, and KRITIS regulations, special attention is given to data privacy and the geographic location of services.  
   - Third-party service providers may need to be listed in Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) with clients.  
   - Licenses and intellectual property (IP) ownership are evaluated, especially for open-source components.  
   - Some services (e.g., Amazon RDS) may not be directly usable for certain customers (e.g., SGB) because the provider could theoretically access plain text data.  
   - Data must be encrypted at rest and in transit, and access to data must be justified and provably restricted.  
   - Compliance with standards like C5, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or ISO 27xxx may be inherited through service selection.  
   - Important legal questions include:  
     - Is data encrypted at rest and in transit?  
     - Who can access the data and why?  
     - Can the effectiveness of security measures be proven?  
     - Are there additional requirements from GDPR, SGB, or KRITIS?

2. **How These Pieces Connect**:  
   The legal criteria are driven by strict regulatory frameworks (GDPR, SGB, KRITIS) that go beyond standard security certifications like C5. Because virtualQ handles sensitive data, any third-party software must not only comply with licensing and IP laws but also ensure that data remains protected from unauthorized access—even theoretical access by cloud providers. This necessitates strong encryption, clear DPAs, and verifiable compliance. Open-source tools are subject to license compatibility reviews to avoid legal contamination or restrictions on virtualQ’s own IP.

3. **Conclusion**:  
   The legal criteria for third-party software and services include compliance with data protection regulations (especially GDPR, SGB, KRITIS), proper licensing and IP ownership (particularly for open-source components), inclusion in DPAs when applicable, data encryption at rest and in transit, minimal and justifiable data access by providers, verifiable security controls, and alignment with recognized compliance standards (e.g., C5, ISO 27xxx).

**Final Answer**:  
The legal criteria for third-party software include:  
- Compliance with GDPR, SGB, and KRITIS regulations;  
- Evaluation of software licenses and intellectual property ownership, especially for open-source components;  
- Inclusion of third-party providers in Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) where required;  
- Data encryption at rest and in transit;  
- Ensuring that third parties cannot (even theoretically) access unencrypted customer data without a valid business reason;  
- Verifiable security measures and potential inheritance of compliance through certified services (e.g., C5, ISO 27xxx);  
- Proactive assessment of whether additional technical or organizational measures are needed based on regulatory requirements.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots. 
Zusammenfassung: 
Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

**Legal criteria that must be checked before a 3rd‑party library, tool or service is used** | # | Criterion | What to verify / ask | Why it matters (legal / regulatory) | |---|-----------|----------------------|--------------------------------------| | 1 | **GDPR compliance** | • Is personal data (EU‑resident data) processed only in jurisdictions that provide an adequate level of protection or under appropriate safeguards (Standard Contractual Clauses, Binding Corporate Rules, etc.)?
• Does the provider offer a GDPR‑compatible data‑processing agreement? | Failure to meet GDPR leads to heavy fines and liability for the data controller (virtualQ). | | 2 | **Geographical location of the service** | • Where are the data‑centres that will store / process the data?
• Are they located inside the EU or in a country with an adequacy decision? | Data may not be transferred to jurisdictions without adequate protection (e.g., US “cloud act” exposure). | | 3 | **Data‑privacy / processing agreements (DPAs)** | • Is the 3rd‑party listed (or can it be listed) in the DPAs that virtualQ shares with its clients?
• Does the contract contain clear roles (controller / processor) and obligations (sub‑processor approvals, audit rights, breach notification, etc.)? | VirtualQ must be able to demonstrate to its customers that any downstream processor is contractually bound to GDPR‑level protection. | | 4 | **Sector‑specific regulatory fit** | • Does the service belong to a certification programme required for the customer (C5, PCI‑DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27xxx, etc.)?
• For SGB‑ or KRITIS‑regulated customers, can the service be used (e.g., managed services that expose plaintext data are prohibited)? | Certain customers cannot use services that are not certified for their regulated environment. | | 5 | **Licensing of the software component** | • Which open‑source / commercial license applies (MIT, Apache‑2.0, GPL‑3.0, etc.)?
• Are the license terms compatible with virtualQ’s business model (e.g., copyleft obligations, distribution restrictions, patent grants)? | Incompatible licenses can create legal exposure (e.g., forced source disclosure, royalty obligations). | | 6 | **Intellectual‑property ownership** | • Who owns the code / any modifications?
• Are there any third‑party patents or trademarks that could be infringed?
• Is there a clear indemnity clause for IP infringement? | Protects virtualQ from IP‑related lawsuits and from losing rights to its own enhancements. | | 7 | **Data‑encryption & access controls** | • Is data encrypted at rest and in transit?
• Who (provider staff, subcontractors) can view the clear‑text data?
• Is there a documented business justification for any such access? | Encryption is often a contractual / regulatory requirement; unauthorized access can breach GDPR Art. 32 and sector‑specific rules. | | 8 | **Ability to prove security measures** | • Does the provider supply audit reports, penetration‑test results, or certifications?
• Can virtualQ obtain evidence of ongoing security monitoring and incident‑response processes? | Demonstrable security is needed for GDPR accountability and for meeting customer‑specific compliance evidence. | | 9 | **Compliance with additional technical/organizational requirements** | • Are there any extra obligations from GDPR, SGB, KRITIS (e.g., data‑locality, segregation, logging, incident‑reporting timelines)?
• Can the provider meet them (e.g., dedicated VPC, on‑prem‑gateway, etc.)? | Failure to satisfy these extra obligations can invalidate a contract with regulated customers. | |10| **Lock‑in / End‑of‑Life (EoL) risk** | • What is the provider’s product‑roadmap and support lifecycle?
• Are data export / migration paths defined in the contract?
• Are there exit‑clauses and data‑deletion guarantees? | Legal risk of being unable to switch providers or retrieve data when the service is discontinued. | ### How the criteria fit together 1. **Data‑protection & location** (GDPR, geo‑location, DPAs) ensure the third‑party does not create unlawful cross‑border transfers or expose data to unauthorized jurisdictions. 2. **Regulatory fit** (C5, PCI‑DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27xxx, SGB, KRITIS) guarantees that the service can be used for customers that are subject to those specific frameworks. 3. **Licensing & IP** protect virtualQ from copyright, patent, and license‑incompatibility problems when integrating open‑source or commercial components. 4. **Security & auditability** (encryption, access rights, proof of controls) provide the evidence required by GDPR Art. 32 and by customers’ own compliance programs. 5. **Operational/legal continuity** (lock‑in/EoL) prevents future legal disputes when the service is terminated or when the provider changes its terms. ### Bottom‑line answer The legal criteria for adopting third‑party software/services are: 1. **GDPR compliance and appropriate data‑processing agreements (DPAs).** 2. **Geographical location of data processing and any required adequacy safeguards.** 3. **Inclusion in the DPAs shared with virtualQ’s customers.** 4. **Fit with sector‑specific certifications (C5, PCI‑DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27xxx, SGB, KRITIS, etc.).** 5. **Clear, compatible software licensing and verified IP ownership.** 6. **Encryption at rest/in transit and a defined, limited data‑access policy.** 7. **Ability to demonstrate the effectiveness of security measures (audit reports, pen‑tests, certifications).** 8. **Compliance with any additional technical/organizational obligations from GDPR, SGB, KRITIS, etc.** 9. **Mitigation of lock‑in and end‑of‑life risks through contractual exit clauses and data‑migration provisions.** Only when **all** of these legal checkpoints are satisfied can a third‑party component be safely incorporated into the virtualQ system.

**Answer** ### 1. What the context tells us | Aspect | Internal Audits & Design Verification | External Audits | |--------|----------------------------------------|-----------------| | **Who performs them** | Head of Engineering, Lead Developer, senior developers (and occasionally other internal stakeholders). | External security advisor, third‑party partners, specialised tooling/services, penetration‑testing firms. | | **When they happen** | At regular “decision points” during implementation (e.g., when a strategic or architectural choice must be made). Also a formal **AWS Well‑Architected Framework** self‑service audit that is run once or twice a year. | On a regular, scheduled basis (often yearly) and ad‑hoc when a partner performs a penetration test or when a compliance‑related external review is required. | | **What they cover** | • Verification that design decisions follow internal guardrails.
• Alignment with the AWS Well‑Architected pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability).
• Identification of technical debt and tracking it in the internal Jira project.
• Validation of code quality through pull‑request reviews. | • Compliance with external regulations (GDPR, KRITIS, NIS2, SGB).
• Security of the **virtualQ** system – both code‑base and live (non‑production) environments.
• Penetration testing and other manual security assessments.
• Validation of the system against industry‑wide best‑practice standards using third‑party tools. | | **Outcome / handling of findings** | Findings become “technical debt” items in the internal Jira project and are prioritised according to criticality. They are addressed by the engineering team as part of the product roadmap. | Findings are also entered into the same technical‑debt Jira project, but they are driven by the external partner’s recommendations and often have a compliance‑driven deadline. They may trigger contractual or legal actions if not remediated. | | **Purpose** | Continuous improvement of internal processes, architectural consistency, and readiness for future roadmap items. | Independent validation that the product meets external security, compliance and regulatory requirements; provides an unbiased view of risk. | ### 2. How the pieces connect - Both audit types feed their results into a **single technical‑debt tracking system (Jira)**, ensuring that any identified shortfall – whether discovered internally or externally – is visible and can be acted upon. - **Internal audits** are embedded in the development workflow (e.g., pull‑request reviews, design‑decision meetings) and are therefore tightly coupled with day‑to‑day engineering activities. - **External audits** rely on **outside expertise or tooling** that can assess the system from a perspective that internal teams might miss (e.g., regulatory compliance, unbiased security posture). They are scheduled less frequently but are mandatory for legal and contractual reasons. ### 3. Key differences | Dimension | Internal Audits | External Audits | |-----------|----------------|-----------------| | **Performer** | Internal staff (engineering leadership, developers). | Independent third‑parties (security advisors, penetration‑testing firms, compliance auditors). | | **Scope** | Design guardrails, internal best‑practice adherence, AWS Well‑Architected pillars, code‑review quality. | Regulatory compliance, overall security posture, verification of the system against external standards. | | **Frequency** | Ongoing – at each strategic decision point and via periodic (1–2×/year) AWS Well‑Architected review. | Periodic (often annual) and ad‑hoc when external partners schedule tests. | | **Perspective** | “How well are we doing according to our own standards?” | “How does the system look to an outsider / regulator?” | | **Driving force** | Continuous improvement, internal technical debt reduction, roadmap alignment. | Legal / contractual obligations, risk mitigation, external validation. | | **Outcome handling** | Integrated into internal roadmap; prioritized by the engineering team. | May require rapid remediation to meet compliance deadlines; can have legal consequences if ignored. | ### 4. Bottom‑line definition - **Internal audits** are **self‑conducted reviews** that focus on verifying that the product’s design, implementation and operational practices follow the organization’s own standards, architectural guardrails, and the AWS Well‑Architected Framework. They are performed by internal engineers and managers and are tightly integrated into the development lifecycle. - **External audits** are **independent assessments** performed by outside security advisors, penetration‑testing partners, or compliance auditors. They evaluate the system against external regulations (GDPR, KRITIS, NIS2, SGB) and industry‑wide security best practices, using third‑party tools or manual testing. Their primary role is to provide an unbiased validation of risk and compliance. In short, **internal audits** drive **continuous internal improvement**, while **external audits** provide **objective, compliance‑oriented validation**. Both are essential, and their findings converge in the same technical‑debt tracking system to ensure that remediation is coordinated and prioritized.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots. 
Zusammenfassung: 
Bessere Benutzererfahrung (User Experience)Höhere Akzeptanz von BotsMöglichkeit zu Entscheiden den nächsten möglichen Termin zu nutzen (normales virtualQ) oder einen Termin zu buchen

response: The legal criteria for 3rd party software include ensuring compliance with GDPR, SGB, and KRITIS regulations, particularly regarding data privacy and the geographic location of services. Special attention is given to whether third-party providers can access data in plain text, as seen with AWS RDS, which is not permissible for SGB customers due to its managed nature. Licenses and IP ownership must allow commercial use and resale of the virtualQ product, and services must support encryption at rest and in transit. Additionally, any third-party service must be evaluable for compliance through audits, certifications (e.g., C5, ISO 27xxx), or penetration tests.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights.
